questions.question: The lifetime of a component of a certain type is a random variable whose probability density function is exponentially distributed with parameter 2. For a randomly picked component of this type, the probability that its lifetime exceeds the expected lifetime (rounded to 2 decimal places) is _________
questions.explanation:
Exponential with [latex]\lambda=2[/latex]: mean = [latex]\frac1\lambda=\frac12[/latex], and [latex]P(X \gt x)=e^{-\lambda x}[/latex].

[latex]P\left(X \gt \frac12\right)=e^{-2\cdot\frac12}=e^{-1}\approx0.37[/latex]

Answer: 0.37

questions.question:
Consider Guwahati (G) and Delhi (D) whose temperatures can be classified as high (G), medium (M) and low (L). Let P([latex]H_{G}[/latex]) denote the probability that Guwahati has high temperature. Similarly, P([latex]M_{G}[/latex]) and P([latex]L_{G}[/latex] ) denotes the probability of Guwahati having medium and low temperatures respectively. Similarly, we use P([latex]H_{D}[/latex]),P([latex]M_{D}[/latex]) and P([latex]L_{D}[/latex]) for Delhi.
The following table gives the conditional probabilities for Delhi's temperature given Guwahati's temperature.

Consider the first row in the table above. The first entry denotes that if Guwahati has high temperature ([latex]H_{G}[/latex]) then the probability of Delhi also having a high temperature ([latex]H_{D}[/latex]) is 0.40; i.e., ([latex]H_{D}[/latex]|[latex]H_{G}[/latex]) = 0.40. Similarly, the next two entries are P([latex]M_{D}[/latex]| [latex]H_{G}[/latex])= 0.48 and P([latex]L_{D}[/latex]|[latex]H_{G}[/latex]) = 0.12. Similarly for the other rows. If it is known that P([latex]H_{G}[/latex])= 0.2, P([latex]M_{G}[/latex])= 0.5, andP([latex]L_{G}[/latex])= 0.3, then the probability (correct to two decimal places) that Guwahati has high temperature given that Delhi has high temperature is _______
questions.explanation:
[latex]P(H_D)=0.2(0.40)+0.5(0.10)+0.3(0.01)=0.08+0.05+0.003=0.133[/latex]

Bayes: [latex]P(H_G\mid H_D)=\frac{0.08}{0.133}\approx0.60[/latex]

Answer: 0.60

questions.question:
Consider the first-order logic sentence
[latex]\varphi \equiv \exists s\exists t\exists u\forall v\forall w\forall x\forall y\varphi (s,t,u,v,w,x,y)[/latex]
where [latex]\varphi (s,t,u,v,w,x,y)[/latex] is a quantifier-free first-order logic formula using only predicate symbols, and possibly equality, but no function symbols. Suppose [latex]\varphi [/latex] has a model with a universe containing 7 elements. Which one of the following statements is necessarily true?

options.A: There exists at least one model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size less than or equal to 3.
options.B: There exists no model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size less than or equal to 3.
options.C: There exists no model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size greater than 7.
options.D: Every model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] has a universe of size equal to 7.

questions.explanation:
The formula has the form [latex]\exists s\,\exists t\,\exists u\,\forall\ldots[/latex] with no function symbols. Take any model and keep only the three elements chosen for s, t, u: universally quantified statements remain true on a subset, so this smaller structure (at most 3 elements) is still a model.

Answer: There exists at least one model with universe of size at most 3

questions.question: Graph G is obtained by adding vertex s to [latex]K_{3,4}[/latex] and making s adjacent to every vertex of [latex]K_{3,4}[/latex]. The minimum number of colours required to edge-colour G is _______
questions.explanation:
s is joined to all 3 + 4 = 7 vertices, so deg(s) = 7, and the edges at s need 7 different colours. So at least 7 colours.

7 is enough: give s's edges colours 1-7. Each vertex of [latex]K_{3,4}[/latex] has degree at most 5 in G and has already used one colour, and the [latex]K_{3,4}[/latex] edges can be coloured with the remaining colours.

Answer: 7

questions.question:
In an examination, a student can choose the order in which two questions (QuesA and QuesB) must be attempted.

If the first question is answered wrong, the student gets zero marks.
If the first question is answered correctly and the second question is not answered correctly, the student gets the marks only for the first question.
If both the questions are answered correctly, the student gets the sum of the marks of the two questions.

The following table shows the probability of correctly answering a question and the marks of the question respectively.

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{question} & \text{probabiloty of answering correctly} & \text{marks} \\ \hline \textsf{QuesA} & 0.8 & 10 \\ \textsf{QuesB} & 0.5 & 20 \end{array}[/latex]

Assuming that the student always wants to maximize her expected marks in the examination, in which order should she attempt the questions and what is the expected marks for that order (assume that the questions are independent)?

options.A: First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 14.
options.B: First QuesB and then QuesA. Expected marks 14.
options.C: First QuesB and then QuesA. Expected marks 22.
options.D: First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 16.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- A first: [latex]0.8\times(10+0.5\times20)=0.8\times20=16[/latex]
- B first: [latex]0.5\times(20+0.8\times10)=0.5\times28=14[/latex]

A first gives more.

Answer: First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 16

questions.question: Let [latex]a_{n}[/latex] represent the number of bit strings of length n containing two consecutive 1s. What is the recurrence relation for [latex]a_{n}[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Split by how the string starts:

- Starts with 0: the remaining n[latex]-[/latex]1 bits need 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]a_{n-1}[/latex]
- Starts with 10: the remaining n[latex]-[/latex]2 bits need 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]a_{n-2}[/latex]
- Starts with 11: already done, rest free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^{n-2}[/latex]

[latex]a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+2^{n-2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]a_{n-2}+a_{n-1}+2^{n-2}[/latex]

questions.question: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let [latex] G [/latex] be any graph with [latex] n [/latex] vertices and chromatic number [latex] k [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

options.A: [latex]G[/latex] contains a complete subgraph with [latex]k[/latex] vertices
options.B: [latex]G[/latex] contains an independent set of size at least [latex]n/k[/latex]
options.D: [latex]G[/latex] contains a vertex of degree at least [latex]k[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Complete subgraph of size k: FALSE. The 5-cycle [latex]C_5[/latex] has [latex]\chi=3[/latex] but no triangle.
- Independent set of size [latex]\ge n/k[/latex]: TRUE. The k colour classes are independent sets covering n vertices, so the largest has at least [latex]n/k[/latex] vertices.
- At least [latex]k(k-1)/2[/latex] edges: TRUE. In a minimum colouring, every pair of colour classes must have an edge between them (otherwise merge the two classes and use [latex]k-1[/latex] colours). That gives [latex]\binom{k}{2}[/latex] edges.
- Vertex of degree [latex]\ge k[/latex]: FALSE. [latex]K_k[/latex] has [latex]\chi=k[/latex] but every degree is [latex]k-1[/latex].

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.question:
Let U = {1, 2,...,n}, where n is a large positive integer greater than 1000. Let k be a positive integer less than n. Let A, B be subsets of U with |A| = |B| = k and [latex] A\cap B=\phi [/latex]. We say that a permutation of U separates A from B if one of the following is true.

- All members of A appear in the permutation before any of the members of B.
- All members of B appear in the permutation before any of the members of A.

How many permutations of U separate A from B?
questions.explanation:
Count the permutations step by step:
- Choose the 2k positions that A [latex]\cup[/latex] B will occupy: [latex]\binom{n}{2k}[/latex]
- Arrange the other [latex]n-2k[/latex] elements in the rest: [latex](n-2k)![/latex]
- In the chosen positions, put all of A first and then B, or B first and then A: 2 ways
- Arrange A among its k places and B among its k places: [latex](k!)^2[/latex]

Total [latex]=2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

Answer: [latex]2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
A binary relation R on [latex]\mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{N}[/latex] is defined as follows: (a,b)R(c,d) if [latex]a \leq c[/latex] or [latex]b \leq d[/latex]. Consider the following propositions:
P: R is reflexive
Q: R is transitive
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Both P and Q are true
options.B: P is true and Q is false.
options.C: P is false and Q is true
options.D: Both P and Q are false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Reflexive: (a, b) R (a, b) since [latex]a\le a[/latex] True
- Transitive fails: (3, 2) R (1, 3) because 2 [latex]\le[/latex] 3, and (1, 3) R (2, 1) because 1 [latex]\le[/latex] 2, but (3, 2) R (2, 1) needs 3 [latex]\le[/latex] 2 or 2 [latex]\le[/latex] 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] both false.

Answer: P is true and Q is false
